items.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016
items.q: And I have them study older players like Louis Armstrong and Sweets, and I tell them I don’t want you to necessarily play like that but I want you to have them in your playing.

ctx.x: Okay. Jazz in academia. Every once in a while your favorite topic — it seems to, every couple of years I think some critic will write jazz is dead. You know the jazz is dead article. And they cite the abysmal record sales and the club scene. But on the other hand, you have jazz in almost every academic institution in the country and you go to Jazz Education Network, those conferences, and do you have a sort of a perspective on the state of jazz?

Yeah. I mean kids that spend a lot of money in jazz school, I’m kind of torn about that because there’s not a lot of work. It’s a really hard living. It’s really hard to make a living just playing. And so kids kind of write and play, or write, play and teach. And now they’re talking about, at Eastman we’re starting to talk about having classes to write music for games and that kind of stuff. So I mean just finding ways to be more versatile. On the other hand, my kids, and I have lovely, lovely people as students,…

— they’re playing really hard music really well. So I think the music can’t do anything but grow and germinate and be better. I’m not pessimistic about it. The business, yes. But they’ll find a way. Because they were saying that when I was coming out of college. “Oh yeah, you’re not going to make a living doing that.” But I’ve had a very nice career of it.
